2.text: The first slaughtering is performed about the beginning or the middle of

3.text: August, according as the fall is late or early. The family is still living at

4.text: its summer camping-place, and the herdsmen bring in the herd, which has

5.text: been absent during the summer. The women of each tent make a fire in

6.text: front of the door. The fire may be lighted from a strike-a-light; but after

7.text: that a spark drilled out with each fire-drill of the family must be added to

8.text: the fire. Then the younger people, men and women, form in line before the

9.text: fire of the principal tent, while the old men go around the herd and assist

10.text: in bringing it nearer the house. The younger people meet the herd with

11.text: loud cries, calling, “Ho hok hok hok!” which is quite like the usual call of

12.text: herdsmen. Some of them, principally the children, shoot toward the herd,

13.text: from their bows, sticks which have had one end burned in the fire; others

14.text: fire off their guns; still others brandish their spears as if about to throw them

15.text: against the reindeer. All these actions are intended to frighten away the evil

16.text: spirits that may have become attached to the herd while it was on strange

17.text: ground, away from the protection of the family charms.

18.text: As mentioned before, the reindeer-herd is not thought to have power in

19.text: itself to repel bad spirits. Elderly men take part in the shooting and shouting,

20.text: only when there are no younger members of the family to act in their stead.

21.text: After this part of the ceremony is over, the first sacrifice is made with small

22.text: pieces of sausage and various kinds of pudding made of pounded leaves and

23.text: plant-stalks. These are thrown in all the “directions” sacrificed to,¹ beginning

24.text: with the dawn. They are also tossed toward the herd.

25.text: Next, some men walk in amidst the herd, picking out animals for slaughter.

26.text: The fawns are stabbed with a knife, in the usual way. For stabbing the larger

27.text: bucks a spear is used; and for each of them an extra female fawn is killed,

28.text: which is laid at its side and called its wife. Most of the other fawns killed

30.text: Well-to-do people slaughter a grown buck for each fire-board which

31.text: belongs to a living male. The poor people kill only a couple of bucks; and

32.text: the poorest, no bucks at all, and sometimes only one fawn, for the blood-

33.text: painting. A dog or two is very frequently killed with the reindeer, and some

34.text: families use dog’s blood for painting. Each slaughtered animal has its head

35.text: pointed in a special “direction,” and its blood is sprinkled around in the

37.text: After the slaughtering is finished, women bring both covered sledges of

38.text: the family and the pole-sledge, and put them in line before the tent at a

39.text: distance from the door. A little farther away are placed two or three sledges

40.text: that serve for carrying the tent-covering. The two groups of sledges are

41.text: arranged with their fronts towards each other. In the space between, or

42.text: upon one of the sledges, fire-drills and the family charms are placed.
